items.title: Semantic Basketball Querying and Temporal Grounding of Play-by-Play Events in Broadcast Video
items.abstract: Basketball play-by-play data provide semi-structured descriptions of game events, but connecting analytical queries to the corresponding moments in broadcast video remains challenging. Towards this direction, this paper presents a semantic framework that integrates basketball play-by-play information into a Knowledge Graph (KG) through the BBall ontology, and links recorded events to temporally grounded video segments using scoreboard-based optical character recognition (OCR). The framework supports multimodal exploitation using structured queries over game events, through the research prototype CourtLens. The latter enables users to retrieve relevant video evidence through a unified semantic interface, including interactive shot charts, filters, SPARQL queries, and natural-language questions through LLM-to-SPARQL. The underlying KG contains 9.5 M play-by-play-related triples covering 1063 games, while the interactive video catalogue currently provides synchronized access to 28 games from 3 EuroLeague seasons. Concerning evaluation, a manually annotated benchmark of 1833 actions from three EuroLeague games yields an overall median absolute temporal error of 4.0 s, with 57.72% and 68.46% of all actions localized within 5 s and 10 s, respectively. Notably, running-clock events (missed/made field goals, assists, rebounds, blocks, steals and turnovers) achieve higher accuracy with 81.04% localized within 5 s and 90.47% within 10 s, demonstrating the system’s effectiveness in temporally grounding actions during active gameplay. Finally, the offline grounding pipeline processes video at 22.74× real time, whereas the interactive CourtLens web application offers real-time interaction for video analysis, e.g., less than 1 s for filter-based search.

items.title: Sequential Gaussian Codebooks for Covariance-Aware Stochastic Latent-State Estimation in Computational Psychiatry
items.abstract: Longitudinal computational psychiatry aims to build computer models that track how a person's hidden mental health state changes over time using incomplete real-world clues like daily symptoms, behavior, physical data, and environment. While standard time-series models are great for tracking changing systems, they often break down when the number of hidden variables is large, measurements are missing, and different types of uncertainty overlap. This paper introduces a new method to estimate these hidden states cleanly and efficiently by breaking down complex updates into a sequence of simple, structured approximations.What Problem This SolvesTracking hidden mental states: In psychiatry, clinicians cannot directly measure a patient's underlying neurobiological or psychological state. Instead, models must infer these hidden states from indirect signals like smartphone usage, heart rate, sleep patterns, and self-reported mood.Handling messy, high-dimensional data: Real-world patient data is often incomplete, noisy, and spans many interacting variables. Updating a model's estimate of a patient's state when new data arrives requires complex calculations that become slow and unreliable as the number of variables grows.Borrowing from data compression: The authors adapt a technique originally designed for compressing images in generative AI. Instead of compressing pixels, they use the same logic to compress and simplify the adjustments a model makes when updating its belief about a patient's mental state.How the Sequential Codebook Method WorksDefining the update target: Whenever new patient data arrives, the model needs to adjust its previous estimate of the patient's hidden state. This adjustment is called the posterior state correction, and the goal is to approximate it using a limited, efficient amount of information.Building a menu of candidate updates: Rather than searching through infinite possibilities to fix its estimate, the model generates several independent "sections," or groups, of random candidate adjustments. Each candidate is shaped to respect the natural correlations and uncertainty patterns among the patient's hidden variables.Picking the best match step by step: In the first section, the model compares all available candidates against the current estimation error (the residual) and picks the single candidate that aligns best with what needs to be fixed. It then subtracts that adjustment and moves to the next section to fix whatever error remains.Predictable error reduction: Under ideal conditions, the authors prove that each sequential step reduces the remaining estimation error by a reliable, predictable fraction. Because each section works independently on the leftover error, adding more sections steadily shrinks the overall mistake at a guaranteed rate.Accounting for real-world digital limits: In theory, the weight given to each chosen candidate could be any continuous number. In practice, computers must round these weights to finite digital values (quantization), so the authors explicitly calculate how this rounding affects accuracy.Real-World Extensions and SafeguardsHandling missing data and shifting conditions: Longitudinal studies frequently suffer from missed check-ins or dead wearable batteries. The framework is expanded to handle missing data types and to remain accurate even when a patient's data patterns shift away from what the model originally expected.Clear rules and failure modes: The authors lay out the exact conditions required for their error-reduction guarantees to hold. They also examine when the model might fail or struggle to tell two different hidden causes apart (identifiability).A roadmap for testing: The authors emphasize that this framework is a proposed research method, not a ready-to-use clinical tool. To prove its worth, it must be tested on unseen patient data, checked for reliable uncertainty estimates, stripped down to test which parts actually matter, and compared directly against traditional tracking models.Core TakeawayBridging statistics and state estimation: The paper's main theoretical breakthrough is linking the statistics of extreme values in random bell-curve samples (Gaussian order statistics) to step-by-step error reduction. This provides a mathematically grounded way to update complex, uncertainty-weighted models of human mental health.

items.title: Sharing Authority - How the GND network strives to integrate further communities to enrich its authority files.
items.abstract: Authority Files in the Age of AI: Building Trustworthy Information Through Collaboration As artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly shapes how we conduct research and retrieve information, the need for trustworthy and reliable information has never been greater. Authority files have long played a vital role in improving precision and recall in information retrieval, traditionally in bibliographic catalogues and increasingly in research data as well. But what potential do they hold for AI applications, and how can they help ensure that AI systems provide reliable information? This presentation explores the role of authority files as a foundation for trustworthy AI applications. It highlights the importance of bringing together the knowledge and expertise of diverse communities to create a broader and more inclusive network of reference entities – without compromising the reliability and quality of the data. Using the cooperative framework of the Gemeinsame Normdatei (GND) as an example, the presentation introduces an integrative infrastructure that enables communities to contribute their expertise to the collaborative creation and maintenance of authority data. Discover how collaboration, shared expertise and reliable authority data can help shape a more trustworthy information landscape in the age of AI. items.title: Sittisart (Rights-Centric Framework): A Foundational Governance Standard for Human Sovereignty in Artificial Intelligence Systems
items.abstract: Modern artificial intelligence paradigm designs overwhelmingly prioritize performance metrics, optimization velocity, and computational efficiency, reducing human oversight to post-hoc compliance mechanisms. This paper presents Sittisart (Rights-Centric Framework), a governance standard engineered to re-establish human sovereignty as the primary, non-negotiable axiom of artificial intelligence architecture. Sittisart posits that human autonomy over personal data, context interpretation, and final decision-making must structurally precede algorithmic performance. We articulate a Four-Layer Rights Architecture (R1–R4)—comprising Data Sovereignty, Consent Integrity, Interpretation Rights, and the Right to Cut—complemented by Three System Integrity Laws. Together, these frameworks define verifiable operational boundaries that prevent opaque inference, silent profiling, and semantic collapse in intelligent systems, establishing a standardized blueprint for privacy-preserving, human-aligned AI deployment.

items.title: Smartglasses Versus Smartphones for Video-Assisted Dispatcher-Guided CPR in Simulated Paediatric Cardiac Arrest
items.abstract: Background/Objectives: Video-assisted CPR (V-CPR) improves the quality of CPR. Nevertheless, the available evidence has focused primarily on adult cardiac arrest scenarios and on compression-dominated resuscitation manoeuvres. In the paediatric setting, where ventilation is critical, the usefulness of V-CPR has scarcely been explored. We aimed to compare V-CPR using smartglasses and/or smartphones with each other and with voice-only assistance via smartphone in a simulated paediatric cardiac arrest. Methods: In this experimental pilot simulation study, thirty-four undergraduate sports science students without BLS training in the previous two years participated in a simulated cardiac arrest of an 8-year-old child, under dispatcher guidance. Participants received video-assistance using smartglasses (VA-SG), video-assistance using a smartphone (VA-Ph), or voice-only assistance (C). They performed 5 min of CPR (30:2 ratio). Assessments included CPR quality, response times, and CPR skills. Results: We showed that VA-Ph and VA-SG outperformed C in most outcomes. Significant differences were observed in the number of effective ventilations (p = 0.010) and chest compressions (CC) at correct depth (p = 0.006). Ventilation quality was 37.1 ± 32.9% in C, 70.1 ± 30.7% in VA-Ph, and 66.3 ± 28.9% in VA-SG (p = 0.038). CC quality reached 55.6 ± 28.0% in C, 74.0 ± 22.9% in VA-Ph, and 77.9 ± 16.6% in VA-SG (p = 0.150). Overall CPR quality was numerically higher in both video-assisted groups, although the difference was not statistically significant. V-CPR also improved correct CC hand placement (p = 0.001) and airway opening (p = 0.036). Response times did not differ significantly between groups. Conclusions: Video-assistance via smartglasses or smartphones improves key components of the quality of dispatcher-guided CPR during simulated paediatric cardiac arrest, doubling effective ventilations and improving the proportion of compressions at correct depth, with no significant differences in time to CPR initiation. Direct scene visualisation gives dispatchers better situational awareness, enabling more accurate, real-time guidance that could translate into higher-quality resuscitation and improved outcomes.

items.title: Socioeconomic Status and AI Use for Schoolwork in Relation to Adolescents’ School Belonging and Loneliness in Four Chinese Regions
items.abstract: Socioeconomic differences in adolescents’ school belonging and school loneliness are important concerns for psychological adjustment. As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes increasingly integrated into schoolwork, its associations with students’ school experiences and the moderating roles of relational resources warrant examination. This study used cross-sectional PISA data from adolescents in four Chinese regions. Unweighted multiple linear regression analyses examined economic, social and cultural status (ESCS) and AI use for schoolwork in relation to school loneliness and school belonging. Family support and peer academic help-seeking were examined separately as moderators of the associations between ESCS and each outcome. All models included sex, age, and school fixed effects. Multiple testing was addressed using the Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) procedure. Higher ESCS and more frequent AI use for schoolwork were associated with lower school loneliness and greater school belonging. Peer academic help-seeking moderated the association between ESCS and school loneliness after FDR correction. The negative association weakened as peer academic help-seeking increased. Family support did not significantly moderate either association, and peer academic help-seeking did not significantly moderate the association between ESCS and school belonging. These findings suggest a limited compensatory role for peer academic help-seeking in socioeconomic differences in school loneliness, providing partial support for the resource compensation perspective.

items.title: Soil salinity: Recent advances and future prospects
items.abstract: Soil salinity is one of the major environmental constraints limiting agricultural productivity and global food security, affecting approximately 833 M ha of land worldwide. Its extent is increasing due to climate change, seawater intrusion, rock weathering, poor irrigation practices, inadequate drainage, groundwater over-extraction, excessive fertiliser use, irrigation with saline water and industrial effluent discharge. Salinity degrades soil structure, reduces nutrient availability, impairs photosynthesis, restricts plant growth and ultimately decreases crop productivity. This review provides a comprehensive and up-to-date synthesis of the causes, impacts, assessment methods and management strategies for soil salinity while highlighting recent advances in biotechnology and precision agriculture. Unlike previous reviews that focus on individual aspects of salinity, this review integrates conventional and emerging approaches within a single framework. Relevant literature was systematically identified and screened using the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) methodology to ensure transparent and comprehensive coverage. Recent advances in salinity assessment include remote sensing, electromagnetic induction (EMI), machine learning and geospatial techniques, enabling accurate large-scale monitoring and management of salt-affected soils. Effective mitigation strategies include improved irrigation and drainage, mulching, chemical amendments, silicon (Si) application, beneficial microorganisms, phytoremediation, nanotechnology and integrated soil management. Biotechnological approaches such as marker-assisted breeding, molecular breeding and CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing have accelerated the development of salt-tolerant crop varieties, including BRRI dhan73, BRRI dhan99, CSR 101 and CSR 104. Future research should prioritise climate-resilient agriculture, sustainable land reclamation, precision farming and artificial intelligence (AI)-driven technologies to enhance long-term salinity management and food security.

items.title: Spatiotemporal shoreline and sea level dynamics along the Kenyan coast (2000–2024): patterns of erosion, accretion, and spatial autocorrelation
items.abstract: Shoreline management in the Western Indian Ocean (WIO) is largely informed by small-scale studies with coarse temporal resolution, potentially obscuring fine spatial patterns and interannual dynamics. This study examines spatiotemporal shoreline change along 400 km of the Kenyan coastline from 2000 to 2024 and tests its association with regional sea-level trend and variability, accounting for spatial dependence. Twenty-five annual Landsat-derived shoreline positions were analyzed using the Digital Shoreline Analysis System (DSAS) along 12,455 transects using Weighted Linear Regression (WLR) weighted by a tide- and registration-based positional uncertainty of approximately 40 to 68 m per epoch. Sea-level predictors were derived from GLORYS12V1 reanalysis at its native grid (47 coastal cells) and tested with Ordinary Least Squares (OLS), a Spatial Lag Model (SLM), and Geographically Weighted Regression (GWR). Results reveal pronounced spatial heterogeneity. The Kilifi and Kwale–Mombasa zones show net accretion (mean WLR 0.57 and 0.51 m yr -1 , respectively), whereas the Tana–Manda zone shows net erosion (mean WLR = −0.92 m yr −1 ), with 36.23% of its transects significantly eroding. The national mean Net Shoreline Movement of +9.45 m obscures this variability. Shoreline change is strongly spatially autocorrelated (Moran’s I = 0.866, p = 0.001) and 12.01% of transects form statistically significant local clusters (6.23% as High–High accretion and 5.57% Low–Low erosion clusters). Neither sea-level trend nor sea-level variability showed a detectable association with shoreline change at the native support of the predictors (OLS R 2 ≤ 0.028, p ≥ 0.26; SLM not significant; GWR adjusted R 2 < 0). At the scales resolved here, shoreline change along the Kenyan coast is therefore not explained by regional sea-level variation and is more plausibly linked to local geomorphic and human factors. National averages must be complemented by spatially explicit, uncertainty-weighted assessments to inform shoreline management policy.

items.title: Study on Quantitative Modeling of Task Completion Probability in AI Agents Using DAG and State-Machine
items.abstract: Autonomous AI agents increasingly decompose user instructions into task lists, but widely used approaches (AutoGPT, BabyAGI, MetaGPT) generate simple linear, ID-ordered sequences that cannot express conditional branching or parallel execution. Newer orchestration frameworks such as LangGraph, the LLM Compiler, and the Claude Agent SDK add DAG (Directed Acyclic Graph) or state-machine execution control for non-linear workflows, yet none provides a quantitative, probabilistic estimate of how likely a plan is to succeed, or how much a redundant (alternative) path improves that likelihood. This study integrates DAG-based dependency modeling, prompt engineering for conditional branching, and a state-machine execution engine, and formulates the resulting task-completion probability P(Goal) with reliability engineering. The model is generalized to 1-out-of-n (parallel) path redundancy and to general DAG topologies with parallel branching and AND-joins, and a cost-constrained redundancy-allocation problem and a Beta-prior estimator of path success probabilities from execution logs are given. Assuming independent task outcomes, Monte Carlo simulations (10,000–100,000 trials) of a retrieval-and-summarization task (72.7% completion for the linear model, 84.4% with redundancy) agree with the closed-form predictions to within 0.18 percentage points across 24 parameter combinations and within 1 point under all conditions. Redundancy at the bottleneck stage yields about 3.9 times the gain at the most reliable stage, as the marginal-utility formula predicts. Alternative paths help most when failures are persistent; correlated failures reduce the gain. items.title: Success Stories of Tech-Savvy Teachers in Crafting Lesson Plans with Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: Teachers increasingly use generative artificial intelligence to prepare lessons, yet few accounts describe how teachers who are comfortable with digital tools do this successfully, what they still need, and how this looks in Philippine schools. This study documented the experiences of tech-savvy teachers in crafting lesson plans with artificial intelligence, the digital competencies they credited for their success, the challenges and strategies they reported, and the institutional support they recommended. A qualitative exploratory-descriptive design was used. Fifteen teachers of languages, mathematics, social science and social studies, organization and management, and agriculture, with 1 year 8 months to 16 years of teaching experience, were recruited through convenience and referral sampling and answered an online open-ended questionnaire. Tool use was summarized with frequencies and percentages, and the 58 written responses were analyzed through thematic analysis. ChatGPT (80%) and Google Gemini (66.7%) were the most used tools. Four themes emerged. First, fourteen teachers described planning with artificial intelligence as faster, easier, and more productive, and two noted effort at the outset, mainly in writing prompts. Second, success was linked to foundational digital literacy, prompt writing, and the ability to evaluate output, used together with teaching judgment. Third, the main challenges were output that did not fit learners, inaccurate information, and over-reliance, which teachers managed by reviewing, verifying, and localizing output. Fourth, teachers asked for continuous training, peer collaboration, and clear guidelines on appropriate use and its declaration. Interpreted through the Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge framework and technology acceptance theory, the findings suggest that these teachers’ success rested on their own judgment, prompting skill, and the support available to them. Because of the small sample, the brevity of many responses, and signs that some responses were machine-assisted, the findings are exploratory and not generalizable.

items.title: Sustainable Entrepreneurial Education and Entrepreneurial Intention in the Generative AI Era
items.abstract: Sustainability-oriented entrepreneurship education is gaining traction, but few studies examine the mechanisms by which learning experiences translate into intentions to create socially and environmentally responsible businesses. Based on Human Capital Theory and the Theory of Planned Behaviour, this research investigates the mediating effect of sustainable opportunity recognition and green creativity sequentially and the moderating effect of Generative AI Literacy for Learning. Partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) was used to analyse the survey responses of 407 students from public and private universities in Punjab, Pakistan. The findings showed a positive correlation between educational exposure and opportunity identification, which is linked to creative idea generation and, in turn, higher entrepreneurial intentions. The indirect (sequential) relationship is significant. Moreover, GenAI literacy strengthens both the education–intention and creativity–intention relationships, suggesting that technological competence complements sustainability-focused learning. These findings complement the existing explanations of entrepreneurial intention by adding an extension of the cognitive and creative process to a technology-related boundary condition. The study also underscores the importance of integrating sustainability problems, opportunities, innovative problem-solving, and responsible leveraging of generative AI into the curriculum, especially for higher education institutions, which are crucial for nurturing entrepreneurial aspirations in today's learning landscape.

items.title: Systematic Literature Review: Digital Transformation with AI Integration in Vocational Education and Practices (2021-2025)
items.abstract: This study aims to examine the challenges, implementation strategies, and benefits of integrating artificial intelligence (AI) into vocational education and practice from 2021 to 2025. A systematic literature review was conducted using the PRISMA approach. Data were collected from the Scopus database. A Total of 17 articles met the inclusion criteria and then were analyzed using the PICOC framework. Findings indicate that the adoption of AI in vocational education and training not only faces technical issues but also challenges related to human readiness, institutional capacity, digital literacy, infrastructure gaps, and unequal access between developed and developing countries. Effective AI implementation requires an integrated strategy involving adaptive curriculum design, continuous training for educators, institutional leadership, industry collaboration, and the development of a supportive digital ecosystem. The integration of AI offers significant benefits in enhancing the quality of learning, the effectiveness of training, competency alignment, and workplace readiness, but its impact depends on how well the technology aligns with pedagogy, institutional readiness, and industry needs. Overall, the success of AI integration cannot be measured only by the technology used, but also by the capabilities of educational institutions and the creation of a collaborative ecosystem that is valuable to industry.

items.title: Teaching Reform of Civil Engineering Construction Course under the Background of AI
items.abstract: With the large-scale implementation of generative artificial intelligence, digital twin, BIM and other technologies in the construction industry, the construction industry is transforming from the traditional manual construction mode to the intelligent construction mode, and the demand for industry post ability has changed significantly. As a core compulsory course of civil engineering undergraduate major, civil engineering construction undertakes the task of imparting professional knowledge such as construction technology, construction organization and site management. The traditional classroom teaching mode has practical contradictions such as lack of practical scenes, lagging update of teaching content, insufficient individualized training of students, and single assessment method. The teaching practice shows that the reasonable introduction of AI auxiliary tools can make up for the shortcomings of traditional teaching field conditions, enrich classroom case resources, and strengthen students’ engineering practice thinking. However, it also faces practical challenges such as students’ excessive dependence on AI output content, professional information distortion, and teachers’ teaching ability can not keep up with technical iteration. This study can provide reference for the digital teaching reform of construction courses in similar engineering majors, and help to cultivate compound civil engineering talents with both traditional construction skills and intelligent construction literacy.

items.title: Technological and Organisational Readiness for Artificial Intelligence Adoption and Organisational Innovation in Deposit Money Banks in Yenagoa, Bayelsa State, Nigeria
items.abstract: Banks in emerging economies are under pressure to deliver faster, more personalised and more efficient digital financial services, yet many struggle to convert investments in artificial intelligence (AI) into innovation. This study examined how two dimensions of AI adoption readiness, technological readiness and organisational readiness, relate to product innovation and process innovation in deposit money banks in Yenagoa, Bayelsa State, Nigeria. Anchored on the Technology Acceptance Model and the Resource-Based View, the study adopted a descriptive, cross-sectional, correlational survey of 400 employees and managers selected through stratified random sampling. Data were analysed with descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation and multiple regression. Respondents rated organisational readiness (M = 3.62), process innovation (M = 3.59), product innovation (M = 3.54) and technological readiness (M = 3.45) above the scale midpoint. Both readiness dimensions correlated strongly and positively with both innovation outcomes (r = .68 to .74, p < .001). In multiple regression, the two predictors jointly explained 57.5% of the variance in product innovation and 56.7% in process innovation, and organisational readiness had the larger standardised coefficient in both models (β = .535 and .444) compared with technological readiness (β = .263 and .353). The findings indicate that technology is necessary but not sufficient for AI-enabled innovation. Banks should pair investment in infrastructure and skills with leadership sponsorship, employee training, a supportive culture and strategic alignment.

items.title: Tecnologías digitales en la educación universitaria: revisión sistemática sobre oportunidades, desafíos y tendencias educativas
items.abstract: Context: The acceleration of digital transformation has reshaped learning environments in higher education and the conditions under which teachers and students engage in the learning process. This transformation creates opportunities while also posing challenges related to digital competencies, equity, and technological governance. Objective: To analyze the opportunities, challenges, and educational trends associated with the use of digital technologies in higher education. Method: A systematic literature review was conducted following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines and the Population, Interest, and Context (PICo) framework. Searches were performed in Scopus, Web of Science, Google Scholar, SciELO, ERIC, and Dialnet. The final corpus comprised 25 empirical studies published between 2022 and September 2026. Results: The findings identified learning flexibility and personalization, the early adoption of generative artificial intelligence, and the growing importance of teachers' digital competence as major educational trends. Disparities in access were also observed, influenced by technological infrastructure and training opportunities. Blended learning and ethical technology governance emerged as key elements in guiding institutional transformation. Conclusions: The effective pedagogical integration of digital technologies in higher education requires coherent institutional policies, continuous professional development for faculty members, and critical digital literacy across the university community. Technological transformation must be accompanied by strategies aimed at narrowing digital access gaps and ensuring educational integration that is contextually relevant, equitable, and responsible.

items.title: The AI Explainability Paradox in Cybersecurity: Does More Explanation Improve or Impair Human Decisions?
items.abstract: Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) has become an important area of research as AI systems are increasingly used to support cybersecurity decisions. Providing explanations for AI-generated recommendations can improve transparency, help users understand system outputs, and support greater confidence in automated decisions. However, increasing the amount of information provided by an AI system may also create additional cognitive demands for users, particularly when explanations contain complex technical information. This paper examines the AI explainability paradox in cybersecurity, focusing on the relationship between explanation complexity, cognitive load, human understanding, and security decision-making. Drawing on existing literature related to explainable AI, cognitive load, human-AI interaction, cybersecurity decision-making, and technology trust, the paper develops a conceptual framework linking AI explanation, information complexity, cognitive load, user understanding, verification behaviour, and decision quality. The paper proposes that effective explainability should not be determined only by the amount of information provided, but also by the ability of users to understand and effectively use that information during security-related decisions. While appropriate explanations may improve transparency and support informed judgement, excessive or technically complex explanations may increase cognitive load and reduce decision effectiveness. The proposed framework provides a foundation for future empirical research examining how different levels of AI explanation influence human cybersecurity decisions and contributes to the development of human-centred explainable AI systems.

items.title: The Algorithmic Consumer: A Theoretical Perspective on Consumer Buying Behavior in Intelligent Markets
items.abstract: Today, businesses are making more and more use of Artificial Intelligent (AI) technologies in their operations. This widespread use of AI technologies is changing how a consumer searches, evaluates and purchases products in the online intelligent markets. Consumer behavior is shaped by consumer’s own cognition as well as influence by machine learning systems (AI technologies). These advanced systems use algorithmic personalization, predictive analysis, ranking systems and automated decision support to guide the consumers. To understand the consumer buying behavior in these intelligent markets, this paper, titled “The Algorithmic Consumer: A Theoretical Perspective on Consumer Buying Behavior in Intelligent Markets,” proposes an integrated conceptual framework. “Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT) (Venkatesh et al. 2003)”, “Diffusion of Innovations (Rogers, 2003)” and “Disruptive Innovation Perspectives (Christensen, 1997)” are the foundations of this research. This paper argues that the algorithmic influence works through three interconnected mechanisms namely, behavioral reinforcement through personalization, cognitive effort reduction and perceived performance enhancement. Here, conventional consumer behavior models are extended by adding new constructs such as algorithmic trust, perceived AI transparency, adaptive habit formation and data-driven social influence. This paper proposes that AI tools and systems do not simply play the role of marketing tools but also actively influence consumer preferences, attention, post-purchase learning and habits. In this work, theory is being built methodologically and conceptual synthesis technique is used. Model abstraction (simplification) and comparison analysis is used to achieve proposed conceptual integration. A through multidisciplinary analysis which included literature from marketing, information systems and innovation studies, was carried out. The aim of this exercise was to identify overlapping theoretical frameworks. With this exercise a nested framework is created that connect behavioral results, psychological mediators and technology affordances. Traditional consumer theories have been used, which focus on the human-centric framework as a base for this exercise. This base was further expanded to understand AI-augmented viewpoint. This study strongly proposes that AI tools & systems are actively involved in the consumer’s decisions-making journey as opposed to the previous conception of them being simply passive actors, guiding consumers. The implications of this study highlight that organizations must manage system transparency, trust alignment and personalization to maximize consumer engagement. This study describes “algorithmic consumer” and its inception. Going further, this study also lays foundation for future empirical studies as well as policy discussions of autonomy, ethics, and control over pricing in the AI-powered digital ecosystems.

items.title: The application of deep learning-based artificial intelligence for accurate lymphatic vessel identification in indocyanine green imaging
items.abstract: Objective: This study aims to develop an artificial intelligence (AI) system based on the U-Net deep learning architecture to automatically identify and stage lymphatic vessels in indocyanine green (ICG) lymphography images, thereby enhancing recognition efficiency and objectivity and assisting in the planning of lymphaticovenular anastomosis (LVA) surgery. Methods: A total of 560 ICG lymphography images from 140 patients with lower-limb lymphedema were collected. After standard preprocessing, the images were randomly split into a training set and a test set in a 7:3 ratio. The U-Net model was used for training, with hyperparameters optimized using a five-fold cross-validation approach. The Adam optimizer was employed for model training. Evaluation metrics included precision, recall, F1 score, and inference time. Results: The model demonstrated excellent performance in identifying lymphatic vessels across lymphedema stages I–IV. The precision scores for each stage were as follows: stage I: 95.29%, stage II: 92.58%, stage III: 93.17%, and stage IV: 90.08%. Recall rates for all stages were above 89%, and all F1 scores exceeded 90%, indicating strong overall accuracy and balance between precision and recall. The average inference time per image was just 56 milliseconds, highlighting the model’s suitability for near-real-time applications. Additionally, the confusion matrix revealed a high discriminative capability across the different lymphedema stages. Conclusion: The U-Net-based AI model demonstrated high accuracy and efficiency in the automatic identification of lymphatic vessels in ICG images, highlighting its strong potential for clinical applications. This system may significantly support LVA surgical planning, enable real-time intraoperative navigation, and serve as a valuable tool for physician training.

items.title: The Digitalisation of Construction (2016–2025): A Critical Narrative Review of BIM, AI, Robotics and Digital Twins: Evidence Maturity, Circular Economy Disconnect and a Research Agenda
items.abstract: Research on construction digitalisation has grown quickly but remains fragmented. This narrative review examines Scopus-indexed journal articles published between 2016 and 2025 on Building Information Modelling (BIM), artificial intelligence (AI), robotics, digital twins and related automation. A pool of 494 records was screened by title, abstract and keywords, and 89 articles were retained. An eligibility audit then separated 78 core studies from 11 records in which digital technology was contextual. The review combines a descriptive profile of the literature with an explicit, criteria based assessment of evidence maturity and of circular economy linkage. This narrative review used a single database and screening by one reviewer. Exclusion followed a construct based relevance test and not study quality. The exact date of the Scopus search was not recorded. Output accelerated after 2022 (74.2% of the 89 articles appeared from 2023 to 2025), 77.5% appeared in two MDPI journals, and author affiliations were concentrated in China and the United Kingdom. Nine overlapping themes emerged, led by BIM for design, coordination and compliance (39 core studies), robotics, automation and additive manufacturing (30), and AI and machine learning (24). Six records addressed circularity or waste reduction, and only two applied a digital tool to a material recovery or waste outcome. Within the retrieved sample, the link to the circular economy is therefore a thin evidence base and not an established finding, and the low count may partly reflect the search strategy. Case studies, pilots and cross sectional surveys are common (19 and 16 of the 89 screened records, respectively), whereas longitudinal studies and multisite validation appear limited. Blockchain evidence in the sample is minimal. A research agenda is proposed for validated, integrated and context-sensitive studies.

items.title: The Dilemma of Authorship in the Age of Artificial Intelligence: Drawing the Line Between AI-Generated and AI-Assisted Works in Copyright Law from a Sri Lankan Perspective
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence has destabilised an assumption embedded in copyright doctrine: that the person who communicates instructions to a machine is also the person who creates the resulting expression. This article examines where Sri Lankan copyright law should draw the line between AI-generated and AI-assisted literary and artistic works. Employing doctrinal and comparative methods, it analyses the Intellectual Property Act, No. 36 of 2003, leading Sri Lankan originality decisions and approaches adopted in the United States, the United Kingdom, the European Union and India. It argues that the statutory requirement of a physical-person author prevents attribution of authorship to an autonomous system, but does not preclude protection for sufficiently original human contributions embodied in an AI-mediated work. It proposes a five-stage Human Creative Contribution Test, proceeding through attribution, expressive specification, effective control and causation, originality, and protection and allocation. The proposed model avoids both automatic copyright for every prompt and indiscriminate denial of protection whenever AI has assisted a human creator. It further recommends evidential disclosure, clarification of partial protection and carefully framed statutory guidance rather than the immediate introduction of machine authorship.

items.title: The effect of response typing speed on trust in AI chat interfaces
items.abstract: Trust in artificial intelligence systems has become increasingly important as these systems assume advisory and decision-support roles. The present studies examine whether the temporal presentation of artificial intelligence (AI) generated responses, specifically typing animation speed, affects trust in chat-based interfaces. In Experiment 1, participants ( N = 71) interacted with three AI agents using pre-scripted question-response pairs detailing different facts about exotic animals. Response presentation speed (slow, fast, or instant) was manipulated within subjects. Results showed that compared to instant presentation, typing animations significantly increased trust in the AI agent but not trust in individual responses. Experiment 2 ( N = 68) employed similar procedures but used a live language model and allowed participants to generate their own questions. Under these more naturalistic conditions, presentation speed influenced both measures of trust, with typing animations consistently producing higher trust than instant presentation. These findings demonstrate that temporal presentation features can systematically shape trust judgments independent of content quality.

items.title: The epistemic limits of generative AI disclosure in scholarly authorship
items.abstract: Generative AI disclosure is commonly treated as a means of making manuscript production transparent. This article argues that its epistemic value is more limited. Authors may accurately report observable operations, retained outputs, and verification procedures, but functional labels such as “language polishing” or “idea generation” cannot fully reconstruct the causal contribution of AI to a finished manuscript. Nevertheless, such descriptions may strongly influence scholarly evaluation. To examine this asymmetry, the article develops the readerly distraction model, distinguishing justified provenance monitoring from disproportionate attention to features insufficiently related to the disclosed operation. Readerly distraction is analytically distinct from evaluative stigma, although disproportionate monitoring may contribute to negative perceptions of originality, competence, or trustworthiness. The model generates testable predictions concerning attention allocation, comprehension, and evaluation, including comparisons between AI assistance and functionally equivalent human mediation. The article further proposes epistemically proportionate reporting through three complementary categories: methodological reporting, governance reporting, and production-provenance disclosure. Reporting requirements should reflect the role of adopted outputs, their epistemic risks, and the procedures used to verify them rather than the quantity of AI involvement. Finally, the article develops accountable judgment as a standard of authorship comprising understanding, verification, decision authority, and answerability. Unlike nominal responsibility, accountable judgment requires capacities and procedures that can be examined when scholarly claims are challenged. Together, these proposals seek to preserve meaningful transparency without allowing speculative technological provenance to displace the evaluation of evidence and reasoning.

items.title: THE EVOLUTION AND IMPACT OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN FOREIGN LANGUAGE EDUCATION
items.abstract: This concept paper explores the evolution and integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) within foreign language education, specifically examining the transition from Computer-Assisted Language Learning (CALL) to Intelligent Computer-Assisted Language Learning (ICALL). Current research indicates that AI technologies, such as Machine Learning (ML) and Natural Language Processing (NLP), are being utilized to provide personalized learning experiences, automated feedback, and sophisticated assessment tools. While these tools demonstrate significant pedagogical benefits, including improved language proficiency and increased learner autonomy, challenges remain regarding teacher preparation, technological reliability, and ethical implications. This paper proposes a framework to effectively integrate AI into pedagogy, repositioning the teacher as a facilitator and mentor in an AI-enhanced environment.

items.title: The Human–AI Resource Dynamics Framework: A Structured Narrative Review of Employee Empowerment and Resource Depletion in AI-Enabled Manufacturing
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping manufacturing work, offering opportunities for employee empowerment while introducing psychological and organizational demands. Using selected PRISMA 2020 reporting items to describe search and study selection, this structured narrative review draws on a final corpus of 16 empirical studies to develop the Human–AI Resource Dynamics (HARD) framework, integrating Conservation of Resources (COR) theory and the Job Demands–Resources (JD–R) model. A theory-informed narrative synthesis identifies two potentially coexisting pathways with uneven empirical support. The Bright Empowering Path links psychological availability, self-efficacy, positive appraisals, and task fit with proactive behavior and performance. The proposed Dark Depleting Path organizes distinct associations involving hindrance appraisal, AI anxiety, job insecurity, and surveillance-related autonomy loss, rather than one empirically validated depletion chain. Individual, organizational, and technological conditions shape these relationships. Evidence for empowerment is comparatively more consistent, whereas depletion findings remain heterogeneous and primarily observational. Methodological diversity, geographical concentration, and limited longitudinal evidence constrain causal and cross-contextual conclusions. HARD provides an AI-specific integrative framework for future empirical testing and human-centered AI implementation within Industry 5.0.

items.title: The liver on high alert: a comprehensive review of antibiotic-induced liver injury
items.abstract: Antibiotic-induced liver injury (AILI) is a heterogeneous subset of drug-induced liver injury (DILI) that ranges from self-limited biochemical abnormalities to acute liver failure and chronic cholestatic or autoimmune-like disease. This narrative review critically evaluates clinical and mechanistic evidence across major antibiotic classes while retaining a drug-centered structure. Human HLA associations, drug-specific T-cell responses, delayed onset, and immune-rich histology support adaptive immunity as a unifying framework for many therapeutic-dose idiosyncratic reactions. Direct evidence, however, varies by drug. Linezolid toxicity and historical high-dose intravenous tetracycline injury are better supported as non-idiosyncratic mitochondrial exceptions. Reactive metabolites, oxidative stress, transporter effects, and inflammatory stress may initiate or amplify injury, but cytotoxicity-only, lipopolysaccharide/TNF-α, animal, and organ-on-chip models do not by themselves reproduce clinical idiosyncratic AILI. In practice, management still requires phenotype classification, exclusion of competing causes, structured causality assessment, prompt withdrawal when feasible, severity-based referral, and avoidance of rechallenge. Biomarkers, pharmacogenomics, patient-specific models, microphysiological systems, and artificial intelligence remain investigational and require validation in adjudicated antibiotic-exposed cohorts with tolerant controls.

items.title: The Majority Report: AI Optimism and Public Support for Police Use of AI in Nine Countries
items.abstract: Police forces increasingly use Artificial Intelligence in support of specific tasks, such as data analysis, identifying suspects and monitoring public spaces. These uses potentially expand the state’s coercive capacity. Yet we know little about how far people accept these tools across political contexts and how these views systematically relate to other attitudes. We ask whether support rests on views of the technology, the problem AI use addresses, or trust in the institution using it. We analyze a preregistered survey of 9,000 respondents in the United States, China, Taiwan, the United Kingdom, and five EU countries using Bayesian multilevel models. Support is high for most uses everywhere. It rests on general AI benefits, perceived crime trends, and trust in the police, which matters similarly across countries. In contrast, general AI risks, personal fear of crime, and trust in legal institutions play no substantive role on average. Acceptance thus primarily is connected with optimism about AI, a general but not personal sense of problem relevance, and trust in the police.

items.title: The Portable Life: Why We'll End Up Carrying Just One Device
items.abstract: This essay argues that the phone and the computer will merge into a single device. Earlier attempts, phones that turn into a computer when plugged into a screen, changed how almost no one works, because the phone had to run desktop apps designed for a mouse and keyboard. The author argues that AI agents change this: once the heavy lifting is something you ask for in plain words, it no longer matters which device you speak from, and the merging of devices follows from a change in how people communicate with machines. Drawing on his own need to reach his agents from anywhere, and on the phone app he built to talk to the terminals where they run, he describes the portable life: staying connected to one's work from any place. The essay examines why the computing power the average user needs is close to fitting in a phone, what still stands in the way (cooling, heat, battery life and the complexity of the processor), and how a foldable phone attached to a screen, a keyboard and a remote could work as a full computer.

items.title: The Roman Dodecahedron: A Handheld Coin Gauge
items.abstract: English This preprint presents a testable functional and ergonomic hypothesis for Gallo-Roman dodecahedra. It proposes that a finger inserted through an undecorated aperture could have acted as an internal tactile stop while a coin was checked against another aperture. The paper distinguishes between gauging an individual coin and the less certain possibility of sorting several coins inside the object. It includes a geometric estimate using an idealized dodecahedron and outlines tests with replicas and measured discs. The analysis does not establish the historical use of the artifacts; it identifies a mechanism that can be tested physically. items.title: The work-family interface and psychological recovery from work: a meta-analysis on two intertwined topics
items.abstract: The work-family interface and psychological recovery from work remained as two parallel topics for many years until scholars started to acknowledge that they are intertwined. In the present study, we advance knowledge on the field by carrying out the first meta-analysis on this topic. A total of 71 studies conducted across the globe were included. We explored whether all types of work-family interaction relate to recovery, and whether the strength of the relationships varies depending on type of recovery. Our findings show that three forms of work-family interaction are significantly related to recovery, namely work-family conflict (WFC), family-work conflict (FWC) and work-family facilitation (WFF). In the case of WFF, the strength of this relationship varies depending on how recovery is conceptualized. For instance, the association is particularly strong when recovery is defined in terms of perceived control over leisure time. From all types of work-family interaction, WFC is the most widely measured, whereas from all forms of recovery, psychological detachment from work seems the most popular. Although recovery has been considered a dynamic process, most of the identified studies are cross-sectional. Based on our results, we identify gaps and present a resource-based theoretical model to guide future research and practice.

items.title: Theoretical framework for the integration of BIM, IoT, and AI in the demolition phase
items.abstract: The demolition phase is one of the least digitally integrated phases in the construction lifecycle, despite its significant environmental, safety, and economic implications. Though extensively studied in design, construction, and operation, the use of Building Information Modeling (BIM), the Internet of Things (IoT), and Artificial Intelligence (AI) in demolition activities has been limited. This paper aims to present a theoretical framework for the integration of BIM, IoT and AI in demolition activities to improve data-informed decision-making and operational efficiency. A synthesis of the present literature on digital technologies in construction is developed to arrive at a conceptual framework. The framework proposes a closed-loop system for demolition, leveraging BIM as the information core, IoT for real-time sensing and data collection, and AI for intelligent analysis and decision-making support. The proposed framework classifies interactions into three phases: pre-demolition assessment, demolition execution and post-demolition assessment. It shows the various layers of data transmission and decision-making hierarchies, it also shows how technologies come together to enable real-time feedback and improved collaboration in demolition activities. The research offers a structured theoretical foundation for the digital transformation of demolition practices and can be the basis for subsequent empirical verification and practical application in sustainable and intelligent demolition management.

items.title: Thinking Outside the Fridge: Specters of Artificial Experience
items.abstract: The world-building capacity of imaginative literature fosters artificial experience through characters who are artificial beings. Interacting with generative AI in natural language also creates a type of artificial experience through algorithmically simulated social cues. Neither type of artificial experience is real in the sense of actually existing, but these artificial experiences can feel authentic. When fiction portrays artificial experiences, it encourages metacognitive reflection. This essay is a meditation on artificial experiences, the bloody business of the human condition, and Gregory Mone’s short story “Bleed.” The short story depicts AI as a specter, as something that is neither fully alive nor inanimate. As the story’s sentient fridge grows increasingly human, its mimicry of human society-almost the same, but not quite-challenges traditional definitions of humanity. In our world, AI may no longer be fictional, but it is shaped by fiction.

items.abstract: This essay examines AI’s transformative impacts through Adam Braver’s short story “According to Alice,” which explores the increasingly blurred boundary between artificial and human in today’s world. While Alice’s creative work speaks to the benefits of human-AI complementarity, her alienation and ennui in both her personal and professional lives underscore the importance of human creativity, collaboration, and agency. Growing concerns about AI in areas such as the labor market, education, and human relationships point to the need for AI that is human-centric and “proworker.” AI’s trajectory is not predetermined but rather needs to be determined by human design and choices at every level: individual, firm, country, and society at large.

items.title: To the Rescue of CNC Operators: An Agentic Approach to Conversational Programming
items.abstract: Programming a Computer Numerical Control (CNC) machine can be challenging. Until now, Classic CNC programming assistants have helped to simplify this process; however, these assistants are generally limited to predefined operations, lack adaptability and often omit preparatory CNC steps. Artificial Intelligence (AI) and conversational agents based on Large Language Models (LLMs) present a significant opportunity to enhance Classic CNC assistants. These technologies enable the development of more versatile solutions, capable of engaging in natural conversations through a prompt-based system. Aligned with this challenge, we present IkasToD, a Task-oriented speech-based Dialogue (ToD) assistant that leverages the language understanding and reasoning capabilities of LLMs, to support CNC operators during the preparatory steps of manufacturing orders. The IkasToD assistant engages in a closed-loop dialogue with the CNC manufacturer’s API to gather preparatory phase information, replying to operator queries, and generating plans to address complex, multi-query questions. These high-level plans based on decision trees extend the system model without the need to redesign the assistant interface. System’s performance is evaluated in a case study from the Elkartek project IKASPROD (Work partially supported by the Basque Government, grant no. KK-2023/00027.), using an in-house dataset with variable scenarios.

items.title: Toward smart management of stored grains: integrating AI, IoT, and climate-resilient pest management for global food security
items.abstract: Maintaining the quality and quantity of cereal grains is fundamental to global food security. However, persistent post-harvest losses caused by insects and vertebrate pests, storage molds, and environmental variability continue to threaten grain availability and safety. Conventional storage systems, which require routine inspection and chemical intervention, are challenged by climate change, emerging pests, and growing demand for safe and sustainable food. This review critically evaluates recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) and Internet of Things (IoT)-based sensors, machine learning (ML), multimodal sensing, decision-support systems, climate-controlled storage, and reduced-risk pest management strategies, with an emphasis on their integration into predictive management systems. The effectiveness of sustainable management strategies, including hermetic storage, biopesticides, diatomaceous earths (DEs), and semiochemical-based approaches, is evaluated with an emphasis on efficacy, scalability, and practical feasibility, focusing on risk-based rather than blanket interventions. Based on these advances, the review proposes a six-stage conceptual framework encompassing the sensing of storage conditions, data analysis, risk prediction, decision-making, targeted intervention, and outcome verification. The central theoretical contribution is the development of a conceptual framework that integrates digital monitoring, climate risk assessment, and sustainable pest management. The framework provides practical guidance for storage managers to identify new risks, choose suitable actions, and assess management outcomes. Major constraints include limited datasets, sensor accuracy, model transferability, interoperability, and cost-effectiveness in smallholder systems. Future priorities include advancing edge and explainable AI, digital twins, and other technologies such as multimodal sensing and low-cost smart storage solutions for resource-constrained regions. Integrating digital technologies, climate adaptation, and sustainable pest management could enable adaptive, predictive stored grain management, reducing post-harvest losses, improving grain quality and safety, and strengthening global food security.

items.title: Toward Sustainable Solvent-Resistant Membranes: Molecular Design, Process Innovation, and Circularity
items.abstract: Solvent-resistant membranes (SRMs) enable energy-efficient molecular separations critical to petrochemical, pharmaceutical, fine chemical, and food processing industries, yet their environmental cost remains poorly addressed. Conventional SRMs are predominantly derived from nonrenewable petroleum-based polymers, fabricated using toxic organic solvents and stabilized through chemical cross-linking agents that generate hazardous waste streams. At end-of-life, the absence of viable recovery or recycling pathways further imposes a heavy environmental burden. With growing emphasis on environmental sustainability and circular economy, advancing high-performance, stable, and sustainable SRMs has become a pressing priority. Guided by the 12 Principles of Green Chemistry as an organizing framework, this Review critically examines recent advancements in sustainable SRMs development across three major directions: (1) green membrane materials, including biobased materials, degradable polymers, and low-impact environmentally friendly cross-linkers, (2) green fabrication processes, including alternative green solvents and environmentally friendly fabrication techniques, and (3) lifecycle-oriented strategies, including degradable and recyclable membrane design as well as artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML)-guided membrane design and performance prediction. By integrating material innovation, process engineering, and lifecycle considerations within a unified green chemistry lens, this Review highlights pathways for developing next-generation, high-performance SRMs with reduced environmental footprint. It further outlines key challenges and opportunities for translating sustainable membrane technologies into industrial practice, supporting cleaner manufacturing and circular-separation technologies.

items.title: Towards a Pedagogical Framework for Integrating Generative AI Into Competency-Based Education in Secondary Schools in the Global South
items.abstract: Secondary education systems across the Global South have adopted competency-based curricula that expect learners to construct knowledge, solve authentic problems, collaborate and demonstrate skills, yet large classes, teacher shortages and limited resources constrain the learner-centered pedagogy that these reforms require. Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has been proposed as a means of closing this gap, but its pedagogical role in competency-based education has not been systematically theorized. Guided by Vygotsky’s social constructivist theory, this study synthesized peer-reviewed and institutional literature published between 2015 and 2025 through a systematic review of 300 sources, selected from 12,125 Scopus and Web of Science records and reported according to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020. The study found that competency-based reforms were constrained by teacher preparation, assessment practices and resources. GenAI offered affordances for scaffolding, dialogue, feedback, authentic task design and teacher support, and randomized trials in Nigeria and Ghana reported meaningful learning gains when GenAI tutoring was structured and supervised. However, unguided access was associated with overreliance and weaker independent performance, and connectivity, language, cost, teacher capacity and policy gaps constrained equitable use. The study proposes the Scaffolded Generative AI for Competency-Based Education (SGAI-CBE) framework, which organizes GenAI use into a six-phase pedagogical cycle anchored in the zone of proximal development, teacher-mediated scaffolding, collaborative knowledge construction, authentic assessment and the gradual fading of AI support, and situates the cycle within enabling conditions and guardrails appropriate for resource-constrained schools.

items.title: Towards Semi-Automatic Benchmarking of Large Language Models for Self-Regulated Language Learning
items.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have become increasingly popular personal assistants for language learning purposes. While exhibiting impressive capabilities on various Natural Language Processing tasks, including text summarisation, paraphrase generation, and question answering, their capacity to provide language learners with pedagogically adequate feedback is less clear. This is due, among other causes, to the lack of annotated data. In this paper, we describe a framework which aims at bridging this gap by (i) collecting manually annotated LLM-generated answers to learners' queries, and (ii) using this data to automatically characterise LLM skills along pedagogical dimensions with respect to a taxonomy of self-regulated LLM uses by language learners. This framework has been used to assess the ability of contemporary mainstream LLMs to generate pedagogically adequate answers to L2 French learners. Preliminary results on a small manually annotated dataset (N = 49) show that establishing a definitive assessment of these models remains elusive; rather, they reveal an absence of consensus among human experts when evaluating models.

items.title: Trade-offs in deploying legal AI: Insights from a public opinion study to guide AI risk management
items.abstract: Generative AI (GenAI) tools are increasingly used for legal tasks, including legal research, drafting documents, and even for legal decision-making. As for other sectors, the use of GenAI in the legal domain comes with various risks and benefits that need to be properly managed to ensure implementation in a way that serves public values and protects human rights. While the EU mandates risk assessment and audits before market introduction for some use cases (e.g., administration of justice), other use cases do not fall under the AI Act’s high-risk classifications (e.g., legal consultation). Further, current risk management practices prioritise expert judgement on risk factor identification and prioritisation without a corresponding legal requirement to consult with affected communities. Seeing the societal importance of the legal sector and the potentially transformative impact of GenAI, the acceptability and legitimacy of GenAI solutions also depend on a better understanding of the risks and benefits citizens associate with the use of GenAI and under which conditions citizens find the use of GenAI in the legal domain acceptable. As a response, this paper presents data from a representative sample of German citizens ( n = 488) outlining citizens’ perspectives on the use of GenAI for two legal tasks: legal consultation and legal mediation. Concretely, we (i) systematically map risks and benefit factors for both legal tasks, (ii) describe predictors that influence risk acceptance of the use of GenAI for those tasks, and (iii) highlight emerging trade-off themes that citizens engage in when weighing up risk acceptability.

items.title: Training on the Use of Artificial Intelligence in Academic Writing for Midwifery Students
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) can support students throughout the academic writing process, and its responsible use requires skills in formulating prompts, verifying information, and checking references. This community engagement activity aimed to describe the implementation and outcomes of a three-hour AI training session for 45 Diploma III midwifery students at STIKES Namira Madina on November 12, 2026. Master’s students from UIN Syekh Ali Hasan Ahmad Addary Padangsidimpuan delivered the training through presentations, discussions, demonstrations, and hands-on exercises using ChatGPT, Gemini, and NotebookLM. The exercises covered selecting research titles, formulating research questions, developing research matrices, outlining proposals, preparing presentation slides, refining academic language, and finding and verifying references. The evaluation drew on interviews with all participants, observations during the exercises, and activity records. All participants reported that the training helped them prepare for their final assignments. Facilitators observed that approximately 75% of participants could independently use AI to support the preparation of the initial sections of a research proposal and could practice verifying journal references. Challenges included difficulties in formulating prompts and verifying information and references, limited access to laptops, and internet connectivity problems. The evaluation suggests that academic writing training should combine hands-on AI use with facilitator guidance and explicit instruction in verification to promote critical and responsible use.

items.title: TriageGPT for DataOps: Large Language Models as Intelligent Incident Classification and Resolution Agents in Data Pipeline Operations
items.abstract: Purpose: This paper presents TriageGPT for DataOps, an architecture in which large language model agents classify data pipeline incidents, retrieve relevant context, and perform constrained autonomous remediation, in order to reduce the manual triage effort that drives incident duration and on-call fatigue. Methodology: TriageGPT combines a retrieval-augmented classification agent that assigns alerts to a data pipeline specific incident taxonomy, a tool-use resolution agent that invokes actions from a vetted, blast-radius-tiered action library, and an audit-logged guardrail layer that gates and can automatically roll back actions, paired with confidence-based human-in-the-loop escalation. We describe the architecture, algorithms and calibration policy, map the design to safety and governance guidance, and report a prototype evaluation on a benchmark pipeline with a fourteen-category taxonomy, 2,800 labeled synthetic incidents and a twelve-week comparative deployment trial. Findings: TriageGPT achieved 94.3 percent top-one classification accuracy and 95.1 percent factual attribution accuracy with retrieval, against 68.4 percent without it. It resolved 71.5 percent of test incidents without human intervention at an incorrect-action rate of 0.6 percent, every one of which the guardrail caught and reversed. In the deployment trial it reduced median time to resolution from 41 minutes under manual on-call practice to 9.8 minutes. Unique Contribution to Theory, Policy and Practice: For theory, the paper treats autonomous remediation as something earned through calibrated confidence and bounded blast radius rather than assumed. For practice, it provides an architecture, algorithms and evaluation method for resolving routine pipeline incidents while deferring the rest to a human with an evidence-grounded case. For policy, it maps autonomous remediation to existing guidance, informing how organizations set guardrails, audit requirements and risk tolerance for AIOps agents.

items.title: Trust for AI Agents — An Ecosystem-LevelFramework
items.abstract: This concept paper addresses ecosystem-level trust for AI agents: what evidence entities need in order to trust each other, and how it can be produced and conveyed. We argue that, as with people, trust is a risk decision on an interaction, based on a variety of information collected in several steps over time. Some of this information is associated with the entities, some with the content and context of the interaction. Unlike people and organisations, digital entities are poor accumulators of trust (ephemeral, mutable, duplicable). Trust in digital entities therefore relies more on the durable entities connected to them (principal, operator, execution environment) and on the content and context of the interaction itself. We also discuss how far this evidence can itself be trusted, and outline directions for further work.

items.title: Use of spatial embeddings in genosoil identification
items.abstract: Genosoils are minimally disturbed reference states within pedogenons, that is, soil units shaped by similar pedogenic processes within the Soil Security framework. They are central to assessing human impacts on soil functions, services, and resistance to threats. Large scale genosoil delineation currently relies on Human Modification Index (HMI) classifications, identifying areas where human modification is on the lower end of the spectrum. In intensively managed landscapes, there may be a lack of genosoils, presenting a problem in studying the condition of soil without a local reference state available. Because similar pedogenic processes may give rise to soils under the same pedogenon classification across geographically distant regions, non-local occurrences may provide an alternative source of reference information. Using the United Kingdom as a case study, we tested whether spatial embeddings (vectorised representations of land surface properties derived from satellite imagery) can detect genosoil signatures at 10 m resolution and whether these signatures can be transferred to regions with limited or absent local low-human-modification examples. We evaluated two satellite foundation-model embedding products, AlphaEarth and Tessera, across three contrasting pedogenons selected from the Global Pedogenon Map. Within each pedogenon, pixels with lower HMI values were generally more similar to the candidate genosoil reference, indicating that the embeddings capture a consistent reference signature in areas with low human modification. At the global scale, similarity to the UK genosoil was largely confined to biogeographically coherent regions. Cross-border substitution of local UK genosoil delineation was mostly limited, with meaningful partial recovery observed primarily in the highly modified agricultural pedogenon. These results indicate that satellite foundation-model embeddings can support higher-resolution genosoil delineation than is currently possible from global human modification products alone, extending the operational framework from 90 to 10 m.

items.title: Useful but Not Always Right: Engineering Students’ Use of ChatGPT for English Language Learning in a Non-Major Classroom in Bangladesh
items.abstract: Generative AI tools such as ChatGPT are now part of how many university students study, but we still know little about how students outside English departments use them to learn English. This exploratory survey looked at engineering students taking a non-major English course at a technical university in northern Bangladesh. Sixty-three students answered an online questionnaire with closed and open-ended items on how they use ChatGPT, what benefits they see and what problems they face. Use was very common: 96.8% had used ChatGPT, 55.6% used it daily and 54.0% used it often or always for English-related tasks, mainly for writing help, assignment preparation and generating ideas. Most students agreed that ChatGPT is easy to use (76.2%), gives useful explanations (73.0%) and saves time (71.4%). At the same time, 76.2% said its answers are not always accurate or relevant, 74.6% wanted more guidance on using it, and 66.7% reported that poor internet access limits regular use. More than half (57.1%) held both views together, finding the explanations useful and the answers unreliable. Students who used ChatGPT more often for English reported greater benefits (ρ = .41) and more over-reliance (ρ = .38), but they were no more likely to notice unreliable output (ρ = −.14). Only 39.7% preferred asking ChatGPT to asking a teacher. Open-ended answers pointed to wrong answers, language that is too advanced, and difficulty writing prompts. Because the sample is small, drawn from one institution and based on self-report, the findings describe students’ experience and not measured gains in proficiency. They suggest that these students need help in judging ChatGPT’s output more than they need encouragement to use it.

items.title: User acceptance of AI-generated cinematic concept art: A multi-dimensional perceptual study in East Asia
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GAI) is rapidly transforming cinematic pre-production by enabling the efficient creation of high-quality concept art. Despite major advances in image generation models, limited research has examined how users cognitively and emotionally evaluate AI-generated cinematic imagery. This study investigated user acceptance of concept art generated by Midjourney v5.2 within East Asian science-fiction and fantasy film contexts through a multi-dimensional perceptual framework. A total of 384 participants, including both design professionals and non-design participants, evaluated AI-generated scenes across five cinematic categories. The proposed framework examined five perceptual dimensions: visual reasonability, narrative potential, aesthetic appeal, immersion, and overall acceptance. Reliability analysis and principal component analysis provided preliminary evidence for the internal consistency and coherent component structure of the measurement instrument. Multiple regression analysis revealed that all four perceptual constructs significantly predicted overall acceptance (R 2 = 0.275, p < 0.001). Among them, visual reasonability emerged as the strongest predictor (β = 0.217), followed by aesthetic appeal (β = 0.187), narrative potential (β = 0.175), and immersion (β = 0.151). Formal moderation analysis further identified expertise-related differences in the predictive roles of selected perceptual dimensions. Visual Reasonability and Immersion were more strongly associated with Overall Acceptance among non-design participants, whereas the effects of Narrative Potential and Aesthetic Appeal did not differ significantly between the two groups. Within the present Midjourney v5.2 and East Asian study context, these findings provide empirical evidence for the perceptual factors associated with user acceptance of AI-generated cinematic imagery and contribute a user-centered basis for further evaluation of human–AI collaborative workflows.
