items.title: Value Sensitive Design Based Approach for Trustworthiness Including Ethics in Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: The lack of trust in artificial intelligence (AI) slows its adoption across industries and society, usually due to limited understanding of how AI works and its advantages, and of how its trustworthiness including its ethical impact are approached during development. Designing and validating a reliable AI system is complex, requiring inputs from various stakeholders throughout the development process. Ensuring that their concerns are systematically addressed remains a challenge. In this paper, a Value Sensitive Design (VSD) based approach to AI trustworthiness including ethics is presented. The rationale of VSD is that since technologies should primarily serve societal needs, the social impact and associated ethical problems should be anticipated by involving stakeholders at the earliest possible stage [ 1 ]. This paper presents a values reference model (VRM) and an implementation method (IM) for Trustworthiness Including Ethics (TIE) defined based on the VSD rationale mentioned. Also, the piloting of the VRM-TIE and of part of the IM-TIE in a use case involving collaborative robots is presented, addressing both technical and human-related characteristics of the AI systems. The preliminary findings in the work suggest that: (1) AI Trustworthiness is a broad concept that must be analysed in detail, considering the industrial context and other priorities, (2) Achieving a shared understanding among stakeholders is essential but difficult, highlighting the need for a structured dialogue, (3) Adopting this VSD based approach, composed by VRM-TIE and IM-TIE, may have a significant impact on the stakeholders’ minds.

items.title: Verification of One Detail Transferred to an Unchecked Interpretation: How a Confirmed Fact Can Lend Its Certainty to a Story
items.abstract: This conceptual paper introduces Verification of One Detail Transferred to an Unchecked Interpretation, a mechanism by which checking one part of an account lends certainty to a wider interpretation even though the evidence for that interpretation stays the same. The paper asks which alternatives a check can distinguish. A finding can support a wider claim when it rules out a rival explanation. Where either explanation would have produced the same result, the choice between them remains open. In 2002, researchers dated the parchment of the Vinland Map to about 1434. A medieval drawing and a modern drawing on that same sheet would both yield the same parchment date. In 2003, a report in Hayadan placed the drawing about fifty years before Columbus’s voyage. The report offered a separate argument about the ink for its claim of authenticity, but gave no independent date for the drawing. In 2021, Yale reported finding modern ink throughout the map’s lines and text. In September 1904, a Berlin commission ruled out deliberate signaling under the conditions in which it examined the horse known as Clever Hans. Carl Stumpf, a commission member, later wrote that many readers understood the report as a declaration that the horse could think. Follow-up experiments by Oskar Pfungst and his colleagues identified an explanation the September examination had left open. Hans responded to small, unintended movements by a person he could see. Part of the Sources and Evidentiary Limits series within On Human Modeling, the paper places this mechanism alongside Tversky and Kahneman’s work on the conjunction fallacy. In a human–AI setting, a reviewer might verify that an assistant quoted a motion exactly from meeting minutes. The same wording could appear whether the motion passed or failed. Verifying the assistant’s further claim that the committee adopted it would require the recorded outcome.

items.title: What Is the “Human” in Human-Centered AI? Restoring the Aesthetic Subject
items.abstract: Human-centered artificial intelligence (HCAI) seeks to orient AI toward human values, autonomy, oversight, safety, and meaningful control. Yet the term “human-centered” leaves a prior question unresolved: what conception of the human is being centered? Much HCAI discourse approaches the human as user, decision-maker, rights-holder, stakeholder, or bearer of preferences and values. These conceptions are indispensable but incomplete. This article argues that HCAI must also recognize the human as an aesthetic subject: a being whose perception, attention, imagination, interpretation, and judgment are formed through experience. As recommendation, personalization, generative AI, and predictive systems increasingly organize the conditions under which people encounter and evaluate the world, AI can participate in forming rather than merely serving human preferences. The article develops the concept of aesthetic agency to describe the human capacity to participate meaningfully in the formation of one’s perceptual, imaginative, interpretive, and evaluative relation to the world. It distinguishes choice from judgment, preference from taste, generation from imagination, and optimization from experience. On this basis, it proposes an aesthetically expanded HCAI organized around openness, plurality, reflectivity, and transformability. To center the human is not only to preserve control over AI, but to preserve the capacity to perceive, imagine, judge, and become otherwise.

items.title: What Kind of Claims Are Transparency, Explainability, and Interpretability? A Definitional Taxonomy for Health AI
items.abstract: UNSTRUCTURED: Transparency, explainability, and interpretability are ubiquitous in the health artificial intelligence (health AI) literature, yet are used inconsistently and often interchangeably. This Viewpoint does not attempt to define the three terms. It asks a prior, meta-level question: what kind of claim do we make when we call a system transparent, explainable, or interpretable? I argue that the three terms pick out three different kinds of claim. A transparency claim is structural: it concerns what can be inspected about a system. An explainability claim is relational: it concerns whether understanding is successfully conveyed to a specified class of observer. An interpretability claim is functional: it concerns whether a bounded human agent can, in principle, re-derive the system's output by following its procedure. I use the framing example of a clinical decision support system that uses machine learning to identify patients at risk of deterioration. I develop each claim type through competing technical accounts, consider salient objections to each, and defend the taxonomy against them. I close by drawing out what the taxonomy implies for the design, evaluation, reporting, and regulation of health AI, and for physician autonomy at the point of care.

items.title: When and how do novice university teachers learn from tensions: a longitudinal multiple case study
items.abstract: Purpose Novice university teachers often start without any formal preparation or education in teaching. This means that they develop their competencies through hands-on teaching experiences. These new and unfamiliar experiences can create tensions. Previous research suggests that tensions may provide opportunities for professional growth, but offers little understanding of how this learning process unfolds. Building on theories of workplace learning, this study aims to explore when and how novice university teachers’ tensions may lead to learning by identifying key antecedents, learning activities and learning mechanisms. Design/methodology/approach A longitudinal multiple case study was conducted including eight junior lecturers. Data were collected via weekly diaries and semi-structured interviews at the beginning and end of the academic year 2023-2024, and analyzed using thematic analysis. Findings The results show that novice university teachers learning from tension depends on a complex interplay between tension characteristics (e.g. intensity), individual antecedents (e.g. perfectionism, self-doubt) and contextual antecedents (e.g. social support). Together, these antecedents enabled or inhibited engagement in learning activities (e.g. collegial conversations), which ultimately fostered diverse learning outcomes through mechanisms such as perspective-taking or social validation. Practical implications The findings provide guidance for higher education policymakers and developers of professional development programs on how to foster supportive learning environments for novice university teachers. Originality/value This study offers in-depth insights into when and how novice university teachers learn from workplace tensions. By linking general theories of workplace learning to the study of tensions, it sheds light on the antecedents, activities and mechanisms that contribute to novice university teachers’ learning from tensions.

items.title: When Physical Interaction Becomes Dialogue: Rethinking Communication, Participation, and Community Restoration in Restorative Justice through Japan's WIND BREAKER
items.abstract: Restorative justice (RJ) places considerable emphasis on dialogue. Yet when dialogue is understood primarily as spoken exchange, the potential of the body as a medium of expression, response, and understanding can be overlooked. Taking the Japanese work WIND BREAKER, first serialized in 2021, as a cultural text, this article examines how bodily confrontation functions in place of spoken dialogue, enabling emotions, lived experiences, and needs for recognition that are difficult to articulate to become intelligible through physical encounters and reciprocal responses. It argues that when the understanding emerging from these encounters receives support from the groups concerned and develops into accountability, the rebuilding of relationships, and the renewal of communal life, the narrative's restorative orientation aligns substantially with RJ's emphasis on community participation and reintegration. Community is understood here both as a network of relationships affected by conflict and as an active participant in witnessing change, supporting acceptance, and sustaining restoration. To extend this argument, the article draws on sign language to demonstrate that dialogue does not require speech and considers international accounts of persons with disabilities participating in restorative processes. These accounts inform an examination of the potential of augmentative and alternative communication tools and artificial intelligence to support autonomous expression. Grounded in conceptual textual interpretation and a discussion of relevant literature, the article neither treats bodily confrontation as evidence of restorative effectiveness in practice nor advocates adopting fighting as an RJ intervention. Whether bodily interaction has restorative significance depends on voluntary and safe participation, opportunities to verify intended meanings, meaningful responses to harm, and the acceptance of responsibility. items.title: When Ten AI Systems Agree, Who Is Still Thinking? Artificial Consensus, Evidence Dependence and the Activation of Boardroom Decisions
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence, Corporate Governance and the Limits of Algorithmic Consensus When ten artificial intelligence systems recommend the same decision, does their agreement provide ten independent assessments — or ten variations of the same underlying assumptions? This question lies at the centre of When Ten AI Systems Agree, Who Is Still Thinking?, an independent conceptual research paper by Dr Birgit Maria Kemphues within International Boardroom Studies and the Decision Non-Closure Research Programme (DNC-RP). As artificial intelligence becomes increasingly integrated into corporate decision-making, executive leadership, strategic planning, financial analysis and enterprise governance, organisations face an emerging challenge: distinguishing computational agreement from independently verified evidence. Large Language Models (LLMs), generative AI applications and multi-agent AI systems can produce consistent recommendations while relying on overlapping training data, shared information sources, correlated errors or common analytical assumptions. Apparent agreement may therefore create a level of confidence that the underlying evidence does not justify. The implications extend beyond technical model performance. They concern how boards of directors, chief executives, investment committees, corporate governance bodies and other institutional decision-makers interpret AI-generated information, challenge recommendations and translate approved decisions into accountable organisational action. Research Focus The paper introduces Artificial Consensus as a proposed institutional decision-making construct. Artificial Consensus describes circumstances in which multiple convergent AI-generated recommendations are interpreted as independent confirmation without adequate verification of their underlying evidentiary independence. The research brings together scholarship on: Artificial intelligence governance and trustworthy AI Large Language Models and correlated model errors Multi-agent systems and collective reasoning Algorithmic decision-making and automation bias Human–AI interaction, reliance and decision confidence Corporate governance, board oversight and executive accountability Strategic decision-making and evidence-based management Organisational decision processes and post-approval activation Existing machine-learning research demonstrates that different AI models can produce correlated errors and that multi-agent systems do not necessarily overcome incomplete information. Research on human–AI decision-making also examines how agreement and disagreement among AI systems may influence human confidence, conformity and verification behaviour. This paper extends that discussion into an institutional setting: what happens when AI-generated agreement becomes part of a consequential corporate decision? Scientific Contribution The central contribution is a conceptual framework distinguishing four elements that should not be treated as interchangeable. 1. Computational Convergence Multiple AI systems produce similar answers, assessments or recommendations. Agreement describes the outputs; it does not establish their correctness or independence. 2. Evidentiary Independence The underlying information, assumptions and potential failure modes must be examined. Different AI providers or model interfaces do not automatically constitute independent verification. 3. Institutional Decision Readiness A board or decision-making authority must determine whether material assumptions have been tested, contradictory evidence has been considered, and responsibilities and conditions have been made sufficiently explicit. 4. Post-Approval Decision Activation Formal authorisation must be distinguished from observable organisational action. A signed resolution does not establish that responsibility has been accepted, an executable first step has commenced or follow-up accountability exists. The framework thereby connects research on AI-generated recommendations with organisational governance without assuming that technical agreement automatically causes decision failure. Connection to Decision Non-Closure (DNC) The study forms part of the wider Decision Non-Closure Research Programme (DNC-RP), originated and directed by Dr Birgit Maria Kemphues. Decision Non-Closure (DNC) examines a specific post-approval condition: a formally authorised decision for which no traceable activation can be established within a defined observation period, provided the available evidence is sufficient to assess the relevant activity. The DNC framework identifies three proposed activation signals: Accepted ownership. A responsible person or function has accepted the first executable obligation. Concrete first action. An identifiable step towards implementation has commenced. Follow-up accountability. A mechanism exists to observe progress, identify blockages and establish responsibility for further action. The present study makes an important theoretical distinction. Artificial Consensus concerns the interpretation and scrutiny of AI-generated recommendations before formal approval. Decision Non-Closure concerns observable organisational activation after formal approval. The possible relationship between these stages is proposed for empirical investigation. It is not presented as an already established causal relationship. Research Methodology The paper develops a conceptual synthesis of contemporary research in machine learning, human–AI interaction and organisational decision-making. It draws on published studies examining correlated errors in large language models, the limitations of collective reasoning in multi-agent systems, AI majority effects on human decisions, model evaluation and governance-related behavioural mechanisms. Five falsifiable research propositions are developed. Two complementary empirical research designs are proposed. Study A — Human–AI Decision Experiment A controlled experimental design would examine whether the presentation of multiple agreeing AI recommendations changes perceived evidentiary independence, confidence, verification behaviour and the identification of unresolved assumptions. The proposed design distinguishes the number of recommendations from the actual independence of their supporting evidence. Study B — Longitudinal Organisational Decision Analysis A subsequent organisational study would examine formally approved decisions over defined observation periods. Its purpose would be to investigate whether unresolved evidentiary dependencies, decision conditions and accountability arrangements are associated with observable patterns of decision activation or potential Decision Non-Closure. The distinction between conceptual propositions and empirical results is maintained throughout the paper. Principal Research Outcomes Outcome 1 — AI agreement requires an independence assessment. A greater number of agreeing AI-generated recommendations does not necessarily provide a greater number of independent evidentiary confirmations. Model diversity, source provenance and error dependence must be examined in relation to the material decision. Outcome 2 — Effective human oversight requires substantive examination. Responsible human oversight is not established merely by placing a person at the final approval stage. Decision-makers require access to underlying assumptions, material contradictions and the evidence necessary to challenge automated recommendations. Outcome 3 — Formal approval and decision activation are distinct governance events. A decision may be authorised without establishing the operational responsibilities needed to begin implementation. Governance examination must distinguish evidentiary justification, institutional authority and observable action. Outcome 4 — The relationship between Artificial Consensus and Decision Non-Closure is empirically testable. The proposed framework identifies specific behavioural, documentary and organisational variables that future studies can measure. The relationship may be supported, limited or rejected by subsequent evidence. Relevance to International Corporate Governance The research addresses questions relevant to organisations integrating artificial intelligence into consequential decision processes, including: Corporate strategy and capital allocation; mergers and acquisitions; investment committee decisions; financial and operational analysis; multinational enterprises; family-owned businesses; institutional investment; board accountability; and the governance of AI-supported executive decisions. Its implications also extend to AI assurance, evidence provenance, algorithmic accountability, model risk management and the design of human oversight within organisations. The paper does not propose that artificial intelligence should be excluded from corporate governance. Instead, it examines how AI-generated information can be used without confusing apparent consensus with independent scrutiny. The governing question is not simply whether ten systems agree. It is what their agreement actually establishes — and who remains responsible for the decision that follows. About the Author Dr Birgit Maria Kemphues is an independent researcher and author, the scientific originator of Decision Non-Closure (DNC), and Research Director of the Decision Non-Closure Research Programme (DNC-RP) within International Boardroom Studies. Her research examines the institutional conditions under which consequential decisions become vulnerable to unresolved assumptions, competing interpretations of authority, inadequate scrutiny and gaps in accountability. Her interdisciplinary work brings together organisational decision theory, international corporate governance, institutional behaviour and emerging AI-supported decision systems. items.title: Who Benefits from Machine Invention? The Right to Science, Artificial Intelligence and the Indian Patent System
items.abstract: Debates on artificial intelligence (AI) and patent law have concentrated on two questions: whether an AI system can be an inventor, and whether AI-related inventions fall within patentable subject matter. A third question has been largely neglected: who benefits from AI inventions, and on what terms? This article examines that question through the human right to participate in and enjoy the benefits of scientific progress and its applications, recognised in Article 27 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and Article 15 of the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights, and authoritatively interpreted by the Committee on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights in General Comment No. 25 (2020). The article argues that AI patents have a dual character. They can advance the right to science by attracting investment, compelling disclosure and diffusing useful applications in health, disability access and education. They can also undermine it by concentrating control over AI in a small number of firms, restricting access to essential applications, limiting follow-on research and offering only thin disclosure of opaque models. Patent filings in generative AI have grown sharply and are dominated by a handful of large enterprises, which sharpens these concerns. The article then shows that Indian law already contains the materials to read the right to science into patent practice. These include Articles 21, 51(c) and 51A(h) of the Constitution; the purposive approach of the Supreme Court in Novartis; the principles in Section 83 of the Patents Act, 1970; the exclusions in Sections 3(b) and 3(k); the disclosure requirement in Section 10 as elaborated by the Computer Related Inventions Guidelines, 2025; the research exemption in Section 47; and the compulsory licensing and government use provisions. The article concludes with recommendations for examination practice, disclosure standards, research exemptions, access mechanisms and a human rights impact lens in AI patent policy.

items.title: Who Gains from an Automated Economy? An Eight-Class, Life-Cycle Model of Consumption, Production, Institutional Capture, and Income and Wealth Inequality in Techoslavakia
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence and robotics can raise output while concentrating its gains among those who own the new capital. This paper asks when that happens, how strongly, and which public choices change the outcome. It builds a transparent synthetic economy, Techoslavakia, with 30 million people in 2026, eight economic classes and eight age groups, and income and wealth Gini coefficients of exactly 0.500. The model links household spending with minimum needs, production with machines that can replace workers, new tasks that create work, a full government budget, a wealth ledger, and explicit measures of diversion, waste and market power. It reproduces the starting national accounts exactly and passes 1,454 automated consistency checks. Nine policy packages are compared over 25 years, and results are tested with Shapley decompositions, one-at-a-time sensitivity variants, 300 global sensitivity draws and a parent–child mobility microsimulation. Under an assumed path in which machines could replace 90 per cent of baseline job-equivalents by 2046, with existing institutions and no compensation, the income Gini rises to 0.581 and the wealth Gini to 0.847 by 2051, poverty doubles to 20.4 per cent and unemployment reaches 42.5 per cent. Losses arise through job displacement, weaker wages and the concentration of automation equity among top owners. Classes 1 to 7 lose 7 to 41 per cent of income against a no-automation path, while the top 1 per cent nearly doubles its income. Income and wealth inequality need not move together, and a lower Gini does not by itself prove higher welfare. A package that combines a public ownership fund, care and education services, taxation of rents and capital income, competition policy and competent administration cuts the income Gini to 0.421 and poverty to 1.1 per cent, and outperforms the no-policy path in all 300 sensitivity draws. The same package under capture loses about half its gains. A 10 per cent robot-use levy raises only about 4 billion crowns a year, while removing an existing robot tax preference raises 60 billion. Hospitality absorbs at most 0.61 million of 9.05 million displaced job-equivalents, so service work cannot by itself replace lost employment. items.title: Workplace Layout Optimization: A Systematic Approach to Minimize Operator Fatigue & Material Handling Bottlenecks
items.abstract: Worker movement and material travel are often combined into one distance indicator, although they describe different physical flows. This paper develops a dual-accounting model for a xyz small manufacturing unit with seven process areas. A synthetic route dataset compares existing and improved arrangements at a common workload of 240 units in twelve batches. Loaded material travel is evaluated independently from empty return walking and ancillary supply movement. The cumulative loaded route decreases from 114 to 50 m per batch, reducing loaded carrier travel from 1,368 to 600 m per reference shift, or 56.14%. Worker travel, including equal-distance returns and explicitly assumed ancillary walks, decreases from 3,456 to 1,440 m, or 58.33%. Part-distance falls from 27,360 to 12,000 unit-metres while the number of material transfers remains unchanged. A geometry-only comparison separates relocation benefits from point-of-use supply assumptions. Sensitivity tests examine unequal route frequencies, return policies, and additional detours. The contribution is a reproducible distinction between route length, carrier-distance, part-distance, and worker-distance. The results demonstrate conditional movement reduction without claiming measured ergonomic improvements, collision reduction, or an implemented factory redesign.

items.title: XevaDB enables AI-driven longitudinal pharmacogenomic modeling in patient-derived xenografts
items.abstract: Patient-derived xenografts (PDXs) are critical models for translational oncology, but their computational use is limited by fragmented pharmacogenomic data, inconsistent response annotations, and poor access to raw longitudinal tumour-volume measurements. Here we present XevaDB (xevadb.ca), a standardized platform designed to support machine learning (ML) and artificial intelligence (AI) applications through the integration of longitudinal treatment and control-arm tumour growth curves with harmonized drug and gene annotations, response metrics, replicate-level experimental design, clinical annotation, and matched molecular profiles. XevaDB provides access to data from 689 PDX models across six tumour types, 69 drugs, 4,828 treatment-control experiments, and matched RNA-seq, copy-number, and mutation data for 337 models. Through four case studies, we show that preserving raw longitudinal response data enables analyses beyond conventional static endpoints: transcriptomic prediction of intrinsic tumour growth, image-based deep learning of drug-response trajectories, replicate-aware transfer learning from cell-line-trained models, and multi-omics prediction of paclitaxel response. These results establish XevaDB as a resource for sharing standardized longitudinal pharmacogenomic data and enabling reproducible AI/ML modeling, demonstrating how integrated PDX data can accelerate computational approaches in preclinical cancer research.

items.abstract: This article examines the internalization of national values among future educational psychologists as a psychological process through which an external cultural norm becomes personally meaningful, emotionally accepted, and autonomously endorsed in professional motivation. The study aimed to describe the cognitive, emotional, and motivational components of internalization and to determine its association with cultural identity. Its scientific significance lies in distinguishing the culturally specific content of national values from general value orientations and cultural identity, and in examining their psychological associations in the context of professional education in Kazakhstan. A purposive convenience sample included third- and fourth-year students enrolled in a Pedagogy and Psychology program at one university (N = 78). A pilot cross-sectional correlational design was used. Component scores from an author-developed internalization questionnaire, a cultural identity index, and motivational indicators were analyzed using descriptive statistics, Pearson correlations, and 95% confidence intervals based on Fisher’s z transformation. Mean scores were M = 3.87 (SD = 0.52) for the cognitive component, M = 3.41 (SD = 0.61) for the emotional component, and M = 3.28 (SD = 0.57) for the motivational component. Internalization was positively associated with cultural identity (r = .62, 95% CI [.46, .74], p < .001). Emotional experience (r = .64) and intrinsic motivation (r = .58) were also positively associated with the integral score; because of conceptual overlap, these associations are not interpreted as independent causal predictors. The study contributes by empirically distinguishing knowledge of a value from its acceptance as an internal regulator of professional behavior. The findings may inform culturally sensitive reflection, analysis of professional ethical cases, and autonomy-supportive learning in the preparation of educational psychologists. Keywords: national values, internalization, cultural identity, emotional acceptance, intrinsic motivation, educational psychologist.

items.title: Развитие аудита в Республике Казахстан: тенденции, проблемы и перспективы в условиях цифровой экономики
items.abstract: The paper analyzes the stages of development of national auditing and substantiates the specific features of the formation of Kazakhstani auditing in the context of the transition to a market economy. The reasons for the crisis of user confidence in audit services are identified. An assessment of the current state of the audit services market in Kazakhstan is provided, and the special role of auditing in the development of entrepreneurship in the republic is demonstrated. The authors identify the gnoseological prerequisites for the emergence of auditing as an independent form of financial control and, based on a retrospective analysis, distinguish models of auditing development. The periodization is examined and the stages of auditing development are classified. A mismatch between the stages of development of national and international auditing is shown, which has influenced the ideology and methodology of auditing in Kazakhstan. The article substantiates the need to transition to a new crisis-oriented stage of development. It highlights the role of auditing as a socially significant activity that ensures the protection of the interests of stakeholders. The special role of auditing as a tool for ensuring the financial and tax security of the state is emphasized. Through a gnoseological approach, the influence of foreign scientific schools on the development of auditing in Kazakhstan is demonstrated. New types of audit services are systematized and defined. Recommendations are provided for the further development of auditing in the Republic of Kazakhstan using artificial intelligence. The study is based on the theoretical foundations of gnoseology, dialectics, a systems approach, historical periodization, analysis, and systematization. The research was conducted in accordance with the principles of comprehensiveness and complexity. Based on the analysis, patterns in the development of auditing activities were identified. The paper presents the evolution of auditing activities and examines the dynamics of the emergence and development of auditing in the republic. Based on logical reasoning, an adjusted model of auditing for the Republic of Kazakhstan is proposed. Keywords: Audit, analysis, regulation, ISA, development, PCA (PSAD), artificial intelligence.

items.abstract: The “black box” nature of large models stands in fundamental tension with the rigid requirement that audit conclusions be traceable, verifiable and reviewable, and this tension has become a bottleneck constraining the large-scale application of audit large models. Drawing on explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) and causal inference, this paper constructs a causal chain-based explainability framework for audit large models, which proceeds in three stages: in the first stage, a natural language processing model extracts voucher entities, and SHAP values quantify the contribution of each feature to the risk score; in the second stage, a causal graph depicts the causal paths among features and distinguishes direct causes from spurious correlations, while a large language model generates counterfactual explanations; in the third stage, the audit report presents the risk level, the confidence of key features and the complete causal chain. A comparison based on an accounts receivable audit scenario shows that this design can turn opaque scores into traceable and verifiable audit evidence chains. The paper further discusses hallucination risks and data governance costs, and proposes countermeasures such as human-in-the-loop review and “T-shaped” talent cultivation.

items.title: “Generate” the Future of Work Through AI: Empirical Evidence from Online Labor Markets
items.abstract: Generative AI is reshaping online labor markets in ways that go beyond simple job displacement. Using evidence from a leading freelance platform around the release of ChatGPT, this study shows that demand falls sharply in markets whose tasks closely match large language model capabilities. Labor supply also declines, but less than demand, leaving remaining freelancers to compete more intensely for fewer jobs. The study also identifies an important adaptive response: Some freelancers shift toward programming-intensive work as generative AI lowers the human-capital barrier to coding. These transitions are not evenly distributed. Higher-skilled freelancers are more likely to make the shift and to preserve or improve their earning efficiency, whereas less-skilled workers face greater risk of being left behind. The findings suggest that platforms and policymakers should treat AI not only as an automation shock but also as a force that redirects labor supply. Effective responses include real-time information about changing demand, targeted reskilling support, and training that builds workers’ capacity to learn and use new AI tools strategically.
topics: Labor market dynamics and wage inequality

items.title: “High demand, low training, moderate trust”: a needs assessment survey of AI integration in clinical medicine education among clinical medicine students
items.abstract: Objective As artificial intelligence increasingly permeates healthcare, it remains unclear whether clinical medicine students are adequately prepared for this transformation. This study aimed to investigate AI awareness, usage patterns, teaching needs, and curriculum expectations among clinical medicine students to inform evidence-based curricular reform. Methods A cross-sectional online survey was administered to 930 individuals affiliated with a medical and pharmaceutical college and its affiliated hospitals; 619 valid responses (94.18% current students/interns) were analyzed using descriptive statistics. Results While 75.93% of respondents were aware of AI applications in healthcare, only 31.99% used AI tools frequently. Although 88.21% acknowledged the necessity of integrating AI into clinical medicine teaching, merely 48.47% reported that their institution offered relevant courses. Moderate trust in AI-assisted diagnosis was expressed by 70.76% of participants. The most desired teaching contents were case analysis and diagnostic simulation (75.61%), drug recommendation and dosage calculation (70.44%), and imaging/pathology recognition (65.91%). Conclusion These findings, derived from a predominantly student sample, highlight a pronounced ‘high demand, low training, moderate trust’ pattern in this vocational college context. A clinically grounded, progressively structured, and practice-oriented AI curriculum may inform curricular reform to prepare students for the AI-driven healthcare era.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

items.title: "I Don't Think It's a Scam": A First Look at Family Intervention Barriers in Elder Abuse Discussions on Reddit and Baidu Tieba
items.abstract: When older adults trust scammers despite warnings, families face obstacles to intervention. Complainants aged 60 and older reported \$4.9 billion in losses in 2024 to the U.S. Internet Crime Complaint Center. To investigate family intervention barriers to elder scams, we collected 2M Reddit posts from May 2021 to June 2026 and 2B Baidu Tieba posts from 2007 to 2026. The final corpora contain 13,082 Reddit posts and 3,933 Baidu Tieba posts, labeled using platform-specific codebooks, manual reference annotations, and LLM coding. Through a mixed-methods analysis, we find that scams often extend beyond a single incident and are reported alongside debt problems and broken family relationships. In 68.0\% of Reddit posts recording reactions, older adults showed resistance or continued involvement; in Baidu Tieba family-confrontation posts, 41.9\% showed continued belief. Relatives identified fraud in 74.4\% of Reddit posts and narrated cases on Baidu Tieba, but without the victim's consent, relatives may lack the legal authority to intervene. In Reddit posts recording reactions, account locks or credential changes appeared in 8.9\% under resistance or continued involvement, compared with 33.3\% under acceptance. Measures such as phone or network monitoring and financial takeover were reported more often under resistance. Recovering funds is very limited in posts recording follow-up results of fraud; Baidu Tieba users reported that police classified older adults' voluntary transfers as civil disputes.
